title: Rules That Keep Players Safe
bigQuestion: How did new rules and new gear make matches safer and fairer?

story.title: The Old Book of Rules
story.kicker: A class opens a history book and finds gloves, masks and mats.
paragraphs: A second-grade teacher sets a big history book on the rug. The cover is green and worn. She opens it to a page with an old drawing. Two men box with bare hands.
"Long ago, boxers wore no gloves," she says. She turns the page. Now there is a pair of puffy leather gloves. "In 1867, a new set of rules asked for these."
She turns more pages. There is a fencing mask made of wire. There is a thick mat for wrestling. There is a list of weights, from light to heavy.
"Each of these came from a rule," she says. "People wrote rules to keep players safe. They wrote rules to make matches fair." A student points at the mask. "When did they start using that?"
story.think: What is one rule at school that keeps you safe?

lessons.title: From Bare Hands to Gloves
lessons.mainIdea: Boxers once fought with bare hands, and later rules asked for gloves.
reading: Jack Broughton was a boxer in London. In 1743, he wrote boxing *rules*. One rule kept a fallen boxer safe. He could not be hit while down. Broughton also used padded *gloves* for practice. In real matches, boxers still used bare hands.

In 1867, the Queensberry Rules asked for gloves in matches. The change took time. In 1892, John L. Sullivan and James J. Corbett boxed with gloves in New Orleans. It was a famous title match under the new rules.

words.d: padded coverings for the hands; boxing rules from 1867 asked boxers to wear them
written directions everyone in a sport agrees to follow

look.title: Broughton's Rule

look.prompt: How did this rule help keep a boxer safe?

check.why: Jack Broughton wrote a set of boxing rules in London in 1743.

check.q: Which rules asked boxers to wear gloves in matches?
check.why: The Queensberry Rules of 1867 asked for gloves in matches.

lessons.title: The Fencing Mask
lessons.mainIdea: Fencers wear a wire mask, and today their touches are counted by electric lights.
reading: Fencers wear a *mask* made of strong wire mesh. It covers the whole face. Masks like this came into use in the 1700s. Before that, fencing practice was much less safe.

Long ago, people watched closely to see each touch. Now a wire runs from each fencer to a box. A light turns on when a blade tip lands. This is *electric scoring*. It came to the Olympics one sword at a time.

words.d: a wire mesh cover that keeps a fencer's face safe
a system of wires and lights that shows when a fencer's blade lands a touch

lessons.title: Groups by Weight
lessons.mainIdea: Weight classes let players meet others close to their own size.
reading: In many combat sports, players are put in groups by how much they weigh. These groups are called *weight classes*. A light player meets another light player. A heavy player meets a heavy player.
Judo came to the Olympics in Tokyo in 1964. It had four groups. Three were weight classes. The fourth was an open group for any weight. Anton Geesink of the Netherlands won the open group.

words.d: a group of players who weigh about the same; they compete against each other

check.why: A weight class groups players who weigh about the same.

check.why: Olympic judo in 1964 had four groups: three weight classes and one open group.

check.q: Who won the open group in judo at Tokyo in 1964?
check.why: Anton Geesink of the Netherlands won the open group in 1964.

lessons.title: Groups That Write the Rules
lessons.mainIdea: World groups write the rule books that referees follow.
reading: Who writes the rules for a sport? Often it is a world group called a *federation*. Many countries belong to it. They agree on one rule book. Then a match in Paris and a match in Chicago use the same rules.

The International Fencing Federation began in Paris in 1913. The International Judo Federation began in 1951. World Taekwondo began in Seoul, South Korea, in 1973. Each one trains referees to use its rules.

words.d: a group of many countries that agree on one set of rules for a sport

lessons.title: Headgear in School Wrestling
lessons.mainIdea: School wrestlers in the United States must wear headgear that covers their ears.
reading: Most U.S. high schools use wrestling rules from the *NFHS*. That stands for the National Federation of State High School Associations. It began in 1920. Its rules say every wrestler must wear *headgear*.

Headgear is a set of hard cups and straps. It covers the ears. It helps keep ears from getting hurt. School wrestling also happens on a thick, padded mat. Olympic wrestlers may choose whether to wear headgear.

words.d: the National Federation of State High School Associations; it writes rules for many U.S. school sports
hard cups and straps that cover a wrestler's ears

look.prompt: Which thing in the bag is headgear? What does it protect?

check.why: Wrestling headgear covers the ears to help keep them from getting hurt.

check.q: Which group writes rules for most U.S. high school wrestling?
check.why: Most U.S. high schools use NFHS wrestling rules.

lessons.title: Doors That Opened
lessons.mainIdea: Over time, rules changed so that girls and women got their own matches.
reading: For a long time, many matches were only for men. Women first fenced at the Olympics in 1924, in Paris. Women's judo joined the Olympics in 1992, in Barcelona, Spain.

In Illinois, girls wrestled on school teams for many years. Most often they wrestled against boys. Then the IHSA made a girls *state final*. The first one was held in 2022. Now girls have their own state champions.

words.d: the last and biggest meet of the school year, where state champions are named
